_comment: What a Clipper video can be ABOUT. Mirrors src/data/cbatGames.js — path and
spokenName must match a real route and the name the hub uses, and a frontend
test asserts that. JSON rather than JS for the same reason categories.json is:
the frontend imports it directly, so there is one list, not two.
Every CBAT game is here, and a frontend test fails if one is missing. That
took adding the site-wide [data-demo-start] / [data-demo-answer] markers to
the ten pages that lacked them: those two attributes are the whole interface
the capture bot has, and without them a game cannot be filmed being played.
Adding a game to the site therefore means marking its start and answer
controls and adding a row here, or the channel can never show it.
answerIntervalMs mirrors the landing wall's demo pool: how often the capture
bot presses an answer control to keep the game looking played. 0 means the
game runs on its own clock and pressing at it would only get in the way.

subjects.what: the site itself: a hub of CBAT-style aptitude games, each with its own leaderboard and score history.
a ranked table per game, weekly and all-time, with your own scores tracked over time.
vector several aircraft through gates and intercept enemy contacts, all by typing compass bearings.
sixty seconds of tracking aircraft, answering maths and identification questions and hitting target shapes at the same time.
the Auditory Capacity Test: track callsigns by ear, steer through the right gates and react to bleeps.
eight panels at once: hunt shapes, match lights, identify aircraft and find codes without dropping any of them.
juggle six aircraft displays at once, holding fuel, speed, sensors, pressure and load drops in tolerance while warnings pile up.
watch a tactical picture of units, aircraft and radio calls build up, then recall the details from memory.
slew a sensor camera onto moving targets and hold three centred frames of each before the pass ends.
a red dot drifting across the display and a crosshair fixed at the centre, held together on a stick, a mouse or a touch pad.
read an aircraft's turn and heading off the board, in two dimensions or three.
mentally weld flat shapes together, or rotate a 3D composite, to pick the figure that matches.
find the target symbol in a grid that grows every round.
read cockpit instruments and call the aircraft's attitude under time pressure.
the Airborne Numerical Test: work out arrival time, distance, fuel or speed against the clock.
two-number arithmetic against the clock, plus, minus, times and divide, across four escalating rounds.
memorise a sequence of digits, then count how many times one of them appeared.
judge the angle on screen quickly and accurately, round after round.
Directions and Distances: follow a journey of relative turns from text alone, then name the direction back to the start.
study the ground one isolated layer at a time, then judge a rotated two-second clip of the whole scene on a single detail.
fifteen tabs of system figures with only two readable at once, and no single tab answering a question.
eight tabs of briefing prose, two readable at once, where every answer needs two of them joined and the plainly-stated one is the trap.
a coordinate grid running minus 17 to plus 17, then a wind sheet read in three steps, both against the clock.
three minutes of clearing coordinates off a 9 by 9 star grid, row first then column, with priority tasks that appear when the job has gone quiet.
